source.title: Analog Physical Systems Can Exhibit Double Descent
source.authors: Sam Dillavou; Jason W. Rocks; Jacob F. Wycoff; Andrea J. Liu; D. Durian

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some equations and figure layouts show minor PDF extraction artifacts, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests data-wise double descent with a physical analog network and digital classifiers, using a different system and hinge-loss measure from the original deep-network model-size claim.
record.gate_note: The paper varies training-set size and reports test classification error and test hinge loss. Its digital comparisons also vary parameter counts. Results cited from other work were not recorded. Training-loss results and output-distribution examples were not included because they do not measure test error.
record.test_reason: A new setting: a physical analog resistor network. At fixed parameter count, the study varies training-set size M and reports test hinge loss and classification error. The test hinge loss is non-monotonic in M, peaking at M≈5, which bears directly on V3 (more data can hurt near the threshold). Small digital two-layer networks serve as comparators under the same sample-size sweep.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. Two refinements: the double descent shown is sample-wise, with parameter count fixed and training-set size varied. The authors also propose the double-descent transition as a benchmark of a hardware system's effective parameter count.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a fixed-size analog physical network and varies training-set size, with overclamping and shifted hinge loss; digital comparisons also vary parameters. This is not the original deep-network model-size experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed test-loss peak depends on overclamping; classification error is monotonic where shifted hinge loss is non-monotonic. Peak location also differs with input dimension and parameter restrictions.

fits_no_version.finding: Peak location departs from the large-system prediction M*=2P (γ*=1/2) in low-dimensional settings. With 2D inputs the CLLN peaks at γ≈6.4 and digital networks at γ≈2. With 16D inputs the peak moves to M*=2P. The authors attribute the shift to finite feature dimension and to bounded, positive-only parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The location of the sample-wise double-descent peak depends on input dimension and parameter constraints, not only on the raw parameter count.

record.problems: The main analog network has fixed size, so it does not test model-wise or epoch-wise descent. The key analog peak is reported for hinge loss, while classification error is monotonic. The no-overclamping result is described as a typical example, and digital comparison values are largely presented in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported test-error results were left out.

untested.parts: There is no model-size sweep at fixed data size reporting test error. The CLLN has a fixed size; the digital runs vary P but report each curve against M.
No test error over training epochs is reported.
The paper does not show risk improving with capacity past interpolation across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across the size, epoch and sample axes. Peak location versus P is reported only for the sample axis.
Label noise is fixed at 7%. Noise level is not varied, and regularization is tuned only to match peak height, not to optimal values. Multiple peaks are not examined.
The paper does not re-plot results against an effective parameter count to show a U-shaped curve.

missing.what: Peak location M* versus parameter count P for the 2D digital networks. M* differs significantly from the theoretical M*=2P, and the experimental M* is shown as a reference line.
Peak location M* versus P for the 16D digital networks, which follows M*=2P.

record.verdict_notes: The tranche is changed from T2 to T3 because the main contribution is a new physical setting. The digital comparisons are closer to T2. Neither original source is this study, so verdicts are allowed. The CLLN peak appears only in hinge loss, not in classification error.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep at a fixed training-set size is reported for the claimed fall-peak-fall pattern.
No test-error sweep over training epochs is reported.
The test uses a shifted hinge loss as well as classification error; its result is specific to the reported tasks, data, and training protocols.
The paper does not isolate risk as capacity grows past interpolation across model classes; its main sweep varies sample size.
The paper discusses effective parameter counts and transition locations, but does not test one effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epoch, and sample axes.
Label noise is fixed at 7% in the reported task; noise levels and optimally tuned regularization are not systematically varied to test peak causes or disappearance.

The paper discusses bounded parameters and effective regularization, but does not show that measuring against an appropriate effective parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Contrastive Local Learning Network (CLLN)
rows.size_stated: 32 edges and 16 nodes; fixed size and parameter count
rows.stage_stated: trained until gate voltages reach a steady value or training error drops to zero
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number M of training datapoints from 1 to 64; reported test classification error across trials.

conditions.value: 7% of training labels flipped; test labels not flipped

rows.value: Monotonic in γ = P/M; test classification error increases as γ increases.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error; error bars smaller than markers.
rows.note: Since γ increases as the training-set size decreases, the reported classification-error trend does not show more samples raising test classification error.
rows.check: The state should be absent, not reversed. Test classification error falls monotonically as M grows, so more data never hurts on this metric. That is the ordinary trend, not an opposite effect. Baseline: training classification error on the same runs.

conditions.value: 7% of training labels flipped; test labels not flipped

rows.value: Strongly non-monotonic in γ, with a peak at γ = 32/5; the test hinge loss drops sharply at larger γ.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error; error bars smaller than markers.
rows.note: Because γ = P/M, increasing M from below the peak region can raise test hinge loss. The paper reports averages across up to hundreds of trials.
rows.check: No fix needed. The peak sits at M=5 (γ=32/5), so raising M from about 2 to 5 raises test hinge loss.

rows.subject: Contrastive Local Learning Network (CLLN)
rows.size_stated: 32 edges and 16 nodes; fixed size and parameter count
rows.operation_detail: Varied training datapoints and measured test hinge error without overclamping.
rows.value: Monotonically increasing test error with γ; the paper reports no convincing double-descent signal without overclamping.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error shown; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The paper says the plotted no-overclamping result is a typical example and that labels as small as those in the main text could not be meaningfully distinguished without overclamping.
rows.check: The state should be absent, not reversed. Without overclamping, test hinge error rises monotonically with γ, with no peak, so more data never hurts. The condition also differs from the main run: label magnitude ρ≈11 mV versus 2.3 mV. The paper calls this curve a 'typical example'.
